title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

hero.subtitle: The lightweight data interchange format that powers the modern web

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, text-based data interchange format derived from the JavaScript programming language. Despite its origins, JSON is language-independent and is supported natively by virtually every programming language.

JSON has become the dominant data format for web APIs, configuration files, and data storage. Its simplicity and readability make it the preferred choice over XML for most modern applications.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for exchanging data between programs. It comes from JavaScript but is language-independent and supported by nearly every programming language. It is now the dominant format for web APIs and configuration files.

sections.title: JSON Grammar
sections.content:
A JSON text is a serialized value. The grammar is extremely simple, consisting of just six structural characters and three literal names.

{ }Begin and end object
[ ]Begin and end array
:Name/value separator (in objects)
,Value separator (between elements)

JSON text exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem MUST be encoded in UTF-8. Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark (BOM) to the beginning of a JSON text. Earlier JSON RFCs also allowed UTF-16 and UTF-32; this specification requires UTF-8 for interchange.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON grammar is small. Braces { } mark objects and brackets [ ] mark arrays. A colon separates a name from its value, and commas separate elements. JSON exchanged between systems must be encoded in UTF-8 with no byte order mark.

sections.title: Values
sections.content:
A JSON value MUST be one of exactly seven types. No other value types are permitted.

objectUnordered collection of name/value pairs: {"key": "value"}
arrayOrdered sequence of values: [1, "two", true]
stringSequence of Unicode characters: "hello world"
numberInteger or floating-point: 42, 3.14, -1, 2.5e10
trueBoolean true literal
falseBoolean false literal
nullRepresents empty/absent value
sections.plainLanguage: A JSON value must be one of seven types: object, array, string, number, true, false or null. No other types are permitted.

sections.title: Objects
sections.content:
An object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs, where names are strings. Object names SHOULD be unique within an object.

JSON Object Example
{
  "name": "RFC 8259",
  "title": "JSON Data Interchange Format",
  "year": 2017,
  "authors": ["T. Bray"],
  "isStandard": true,
  "obsoletedBy": null
}

The specification says names SHOULD be unique, and the behavior of software that receives an object with duplicate names is unpredictable. Different parsers may take the first value, take the last value, or reject the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A JSON object is an unordered collection of name and value pairs, where each name is a string. Names should be unique within an object. If they are not, software behaves unpredictably: parsers may take the first value, take the last, or reject the document.

sections.title: Arrays
sections.content:
An array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values. Array elements do not need to be of the same type.

JSON Array Examples
// Homogeneous array
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

// Heterogeneous array
["hello", 42, true, null, {"key": "val"}]

// Nested arrays
[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]

// Empty array
[]
sections.plainLanguage: A JSON array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values. The values do not have to be of the same type, and arrays can be nested inside each other.

sections.title: Strings
sections.content:
A string is a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters, wrapped in double quotes. Several characters must be escaped using a backslash.

\"Quotation markU+0022
\\Reverse solidus (backslash)U+005C
\nNewline (line feed)U+000A
\tHorizontal tabU+0009
\uXXXXUnicode escape sequenceAny BMP char

JSON strings MUST use double quotes. Single quotes are not valid JSON. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (like emoji) must be encoded as a UTF-16 surrogate pair using two \uXXXX escapes.
sections.plainLanguage: A JSON string is zero or more Unicode characters inside double quotes. Single quotes are not valid. Some characters, such as the quote itself and the backslash, must be escaped with a backslash. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane are written as a pair of \u escapes.

sections.title: Numbers
sections.content:
JSON numbers follow a decimal format. Leading zeros are not permitted (except in 0.x notation), and special values like NaN and Infinity are not valid JSON.

Valid JSON Numbers
42          // integer
-17         // negative
3.14159     // decimal
2.998e8     // scientific notation
-1.6e-19    // negative with exponent
0           // zero

JSON does not distinguish between integers and floating-point numbers. Implementations that use IEEE 754 double-precision (like JavaScript) can only represent integers exactly up to 2^53. For larger numbers, use strings instead.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON numbers use plain decimal notation, with optional fraction and exponent. Leading zeros, NaN and Infinity are not allowed. JSON does not separate integers from floating-point numbers. Software using double-precision floats is exact only up to 2^53, so larger integers should be written as strings.

subtitle: The lightweight data interchange format that powers the modern web
summary: JSON is a small text format for sending structured data between programs. It has objects, arrays, strings, numbers and three literal names (true, false and null), and it must be written in UTF-8. RFC 8259 is the Internet Standard that pins down the grammar and the rules for encoding and interoperating.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON is a small text format for sending structured data between programs. It has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, and the literal names true, false and null, and it must be written in UTF-8. RFC 8259 is the Internet Standard that fixes the grammar and interoperability rules.

tldr.problem: Programs written in different languages need to swap structured data without a heavy or ambiguous format.
tldr.mechanism: Text built from objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null, encoded as UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: A grammar small enough to implement in any language, which made it the default format for web APIs and configuration.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: UTF-8, no BOM (for interchange outside closed ecosystems)

facts.label: Value types
facts.value: object, array, string, number, true, false, null

today: JSON is the default payload format for web APIs, and it is also common in configuration files and document databases. Every mainstream language ships a JSON parser, and browsers expose JSON.parse and JSON.stringify. Related formats such as JSON Lines and JSON5 build on or loosen it, but strict JSON as defined here is what interoperable software exchanges.

implementations.name: JSON.parse / JSON.stringify
implementations.note: Built into JavaScript engines in every browser and in Node.js.
